items.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: So we’d back up whoever they would bring in. ... So we did a couple of nights with Ella so I got to play with Tommy Flanagan and Keter Betts

ctx.x: Absolutely. A lot of traditional. Because especially banjo, it’s playing rhythm, it’s playing time down and laying time down. And a good rhythm player, and that could be a bass player or whatever, you should be able to hold the fort whether anybody else is playing or not. So I do a lot of jobs where there is not a drummer. Duo gigs, even when there’s no bass player, because I can hold the fort. I don’t need to have a drummer doing this. But when you’ve got a guy like Tony [DeNicola], I mean that’s like, oh man…

— you just go along for the ride, that just is so easy when it’s like that. But you get the idea. So yeah, I mean a lot of different things. Sometimes traditional Dixie kind of things like for school programs for elementary school kids during the day, concerts with Jazz at Lincoln Center, we did the “Rhapsody in Blue” with Marcus Roberts and then we started out with Ferde Grofe’s original orchestration which is banjo, but then he opens it up in the middle and changes it around so you’re reading the original banjo…
